questions.question: Before joining a trial, participants must give their informed:
questions.explanation: Informed consent — understanding and voluntarily agreeing to the trial — is a core ethical requirement of human research.

questions.question: The main aim of a Phase I trial is to assess a drug's safety, tolerability and:
questions.explanation: Phase I focuses on how the body handles the drug (pharmacokinetics) and what doses are safely tolerated.

questions.question: Phase II trials move into patients with the disease chiefly to test early efficacy and:
questions.explanation: Phase II looks for signs the drug works and helps choose the dose to carry into larger trials.

questions.question: Phase III is called the pivotal test because it provides large-scale, controlled evidence of efficacy and:
questions.explanation: Phase III enrols many patients in controlled trials to confirm both efficacy and safety before approval is sought.

questions.question: Phase I typically uses healthy volunteers rather than patients so that early observations reflect the drug and not the:
questions.explanation: Using healthy volunteers lets investigators study safety and handling of the drug without confounding by the disease itself.

questions.question: Across the whole pipeline, roughly what fraction of discovery projects become a marketed drug?
questions.explanation: Only about 1 in 100 discovery projects survives the funnel to become an approved, marketed medicine.

questions.question: The international ethical and quality standard governing how trials are run is known as:
questions.explanation: ICH Good Clinical Practice (GCP) sets the ethical and scientific quality standards for designing and conducting trials.

questions.question: A controlled trial compares the new treatment against a control group to reveal the drug's:
questions.explanation: Comparing with a control (placebo or standard care) isolates the drug's genuine effect from natural change and expectation.

questions.question: Detecting a rare side effect only after a drug is widely marketed is the job of:
questions.explanation: Pharmacovigilance monitors safety in the marketed population, catching rare harms that trials were too small to reveal.

questions.question: Randomly assigning participants to treatment or control groups mainly serves to:
questions.explanation: Randomisation balances known and unknown differences between groups, so any outcome difference can be attributed to the treatment.

questions.question: Keeping participants unaware of whether they receive drug or placebo (blinding) chiefly reduces:
questions.explanation: Blinding prevents participants' expectations from colouring reported outcomes, reducing bias in the comparison.

questions.question: COVID-19 vaccines were developed unusually quickly mainly because developers:
questions.explanation: Massive upfront funding let developers overlap normally sequential steps and manufacture at risk, without skipping any trial phase.

questions.question: Placing the phases in order, first-in-human safety comes before efficacy-and-dose, which comes before the:
questions.explanation: Phase I (safety) precedes Phase II (efficacy/dose), which precedes the large Phase III pivotal controlled trial.

questions.question: Trials are run in ascending phases mainly so that expensive, large studies are done only on drugs that have already shown:
questions.explanation: The staged design is a cost-and-risk filter: cheap questions on few people first, so big Phase III studies run only on de-risked candidates.

questions.question: If about 10 candidates enter Phase I and 1 is approved, the success rate from first-in-human to market is about:
questions.explanation: One approval from ten entering human trials is roughly a 10% success rate for first-in-human candidates.

questions.question: The existence of a genuine placebo effect is the main reason a new drug must be shown to be better than:
questions.explanation: Because inactive treatment can itself produce improvement, a drug must beat a placebo comparator to prove a real pharmacological effect.

questions.question: A harm occurring once in 10,000 users may be missed before approval because Phase III typically enrols only:
questions.explanation: With at most a few thousand participants, Phase III cannot reliably detect a 1-in-10,000 event, which is why Phase IV surveillance is needed.

questions.question: A Phase 0 study gives participants a tiny 'micro-dose' mainly to gather very early data on:
questions.explanation: Phase 0 uses sub-therapeutic micro-doses to see how the drug behaves in humans before committing to full Phase I.

questions.question: An independent ethics committee reviews a trial protocol primarily to protect the:
questions.explanation: Ethics committees judge whether risks to participants are justified and consent is adequate, safeguarding the people in the trial.

questions.question: Manufacturing COVID-19 vaccines 'at risk' during trials meant companies:
questions.explanation: At-risk manufacturing built stockpiles before knowing if the vaccine would be approved, saving time without bypassing any safety phase.

questions.question: Describing a clinical trial as 'prospective' means outcomes are followed:
options: D. after the drug is banned
questions.explanation: A prospective trial defines the intervention and then follows participants forward in time to measure predetermined outcomes.

questions.question: On the development map, clinical trials sit between preclinical development and:
questions.explanation: Human trials follow preclinical work and precede regulatory approval, after which Phase IV surveillance continues.

pharmacogenomics_medi2004_wk7.html.title: MEDI2004 W7 · Pharmacogenomics
pharmacogenomics_medi2004_wk7.html.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
pharmacogenomics_medi2004_wk7.html.content: Pharmacogenomics — how inherited genetic variation shapes drug response. Genetic factors account for 20–95% of the variability between patients, alongside disease state, age, gender, weight, diet and drug interactions. Raw material: mutations, polymorphisms (a variant carried by more than 1% of a population) and single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Pharmacogenetics classically means one gene; pharmacogenomics means genome-wide, though the terms are used interchangeably. Variation splits into pharmacodynamic (in the drug TARGET) and pharmacokinetic (in drug DISPOSITION). PD examples: the µ-opioid receptor A118G variant alters opioid response; VKORC1 variants change warfarin sensitivity, since warfarin's target is vitamin-K epoxide reductase. PK examples: CYP2D6 metaboliser phenotypes — poor, intermediate, normal and ultra-rapid. Codeine is a prodrug activated by CYP2D6 to morphine: poor metabolisers get little analgesia, while ultra-rapid metabolisers can suffer dangerous respiratory depression from a standard dose. Tamoxifen is a prodrug needing CYP2D6 to form active endoxifen; nortriptyline levels also track CYP2D6. P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) variants affect digoxin handling. The goal is precision medicine — read the genotype first, then match the right drug and dose to the right patient.

questions.question: Pharmacogenomics is the study of how a patient's drug response is shaped by their:
questions.explanation: Pharmacogenomics examines how inherited genetic variation affects the way a person responds to drugs.

questions.question: A single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) is a variation affecting:
questions.explanation: A SNP is a difference at a single nucleotide (DNA base) in the genome, the commonest form of genetic variation.

questions.question: Codeine only relieves pain well after it is converted by CYP2D6 into:
questions.explanation: Codeine is a prodrug; CYP2D6 converts it to morphine, the metabolite responsible for most of its analgesic effect.

questions.question: Precision (personalised) medicine aims to match the drug and dose to each patient's:
questions.explanation: Precision medicine uses a patient's genetic profile to choose the most effective and safest drug and dose.

questions.question: Roughly what share of the variability in drug response between patients is attributed to genetic factors?
questions.explanation: Genetic factors are estimated to account for 20–95% of between-patient variability, the largest single contributor.

questions.question: A CYP2D6 poor metaboliser given standard-dose codeine is most likely to experience:
questions.explanation: Poor metabolisers make little morphine from codeine, so they get inadequate analgesia at the usual dose.

questions.question: A CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metaboliser taking normal-dose codeine is at particular risk of:
questions.explanation: Ultra-rapid metabolisers convert codeine to morphine very quickly, so a standard dose can cause dangerous opioid toxicity.

questions.question: A genetic difference in a CYP450 enzyme that changes how fast a drug is cleared is a form of variation in:
questions.explanation: Variation in metabolising enzymes changes drug disposition (pharmacokinetics) — how the body handles the drug — rather than the target.

questions.question: A polymorphism in the µ-opioid receptor that changes a patient's response to morphine is variation in the:
questions.explanation: The receptor is the drug's target, so a variant there is pharmacodynamic variation — altering the effect for a given concentration.

questions.question: Variants in VKORC1 alter a patient's warfarin requirement because VKORC1 encodes warfarin's:
questions.explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin-K epoxide reductase (VKORC1); variants change target sensitivity, so the effective dose differs between patients.

questions.question: A genetic variant is formally called a polymorphism when it is present in a population at a frequency above:
questions.explanation: By convention a variant carried by more than 1% of a population is a polymorphism, distinguishing it from a rare mutation.

questions.question: Tamoxifen depends on CYP2D6 to form its active metabolite. Tamoxifen is therefore a:
questions.explanation: Tamoxifen must be metabolised by CYP2D6 to active endoxifen, so it is a prodrug whose benefit depends on that enzyme's activity.

questions.question: A breast-cancer patient who is a CYP2D6 poor metaboliser may get less benefit from tamoxifen because she forms less:
questions.explanation: CYP2D6 activates tamoxifen to endoxifen; poor metabolisers form less endoxifen, potentially reducing the drug's effectiveness.

questions.question: The term 'pharmacogenetics' classically refers to the effect on drug response of:
questions.explanation: Pharmacogenetics classically studies one gene's effect, whereas pharmacogenomics takes a genome-wide view; the terms now overlap.

questions.question: Variants in the ABCB1 gene affect digoxin levels because ABCB1 encodes the efflux transporter:
questions.explanation: ABCB1 encodes P-glycoprotein, which effluxes digoxin; variants change transport and hence plasma digoxin concentrations.

questions.question: Besides genetics, which factor also shifts an individual's response to a drug?
questions.explanation: Disease state such as liver dysfunction is one of several non-genetic factors — with age, weight, diet and interactions — that alter drug response.

questions.question: Compared with a polymorphism, a mutation is generally distinguished by being:
questions.explanation: A mutation is a less common change (typically under 1% frequency); once a variant becomes common it is termed a polymorphism.

questions.question: Why did regulators warn against giving codeine to some breastfeeding mothers who are ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolisers?
questions.explanation: Ultra-rapid metabolisers produce excess morphine, which can reach breast milk in amounts high enough to harm a nursing infant.

questions.question: For a drug that is INACTIVATED by CYP2D6 (not a prodrug), a poor metaboliser is most likely to show:
questions.explanation: If the enzyme normally clears the active drug, a poor metaboliser clears it slowly, so levels rise — the opposite of the prodrug case.

questions.question: A patient with a CYP2C9 variant that slows warfarin metabolism will generally need a warfarin dose that is:
questions.explanation: Slower metabolism raises warfarin exposure, so a lower dose achieves target anticoagulation and avoids bleeding.

questions.question: A patient clears a drug at a completely normal rate yet responds poorly to it. The most likely genetic explanation lies in the:
questions.explanation: Normal clearance points away from pharmacokinetics; poor response despite adequate levels suggests a variant in the drug's target (pharmacodynamic).

questions.question: The strongest argument for genotyping a patient BEFORE prescribing is that it can:
questions.explanation: Pre-treatment genotyping identifies patients at risk of poor response or toxicity before the drug is given, its key advantage over reacting afterwards.

questions.question: Two patients on the identical dose show opposite outcomes — one toxicity, one no effect. Pharmacogenomics attributes this chiefly to differences in their:
questions.explanation: Inherited variants in enzymes, transporters or targets can push two patients to opposite extremes on the same dose — the core lesson of the field.

questions.question: The µ-opioid receptor A118G variant is best classified as a source of variation in drug:
questions.explanation: A118G alters the receptor itself, so it changes the pharmacodynamic response to opioids rather than their pharmacokinetics.

questions.question: Genotyping CYP2D6 helps most for drugs that are:
questions.explanation: Only drugs metabolised by CYP2D6 are affected by its genotype; a drug cleared by other routes is unaffected by CYP2D6 status.

questions.question: For a prodrug activated by an enzyme, an ultra-rapid metaboliser phenotype tends to produce:
questions.explanation: Faster activation makes more of the active metabolite, which is why ultra-rapid metabolisers can overshoot with prodrugs like codeine.

questions.question: A study screening the entire genome for variants linked to a drug reaction is best described as:
questions.explanation: Surveying the whole genome is the pharmacogenomic (genome-wide) approach, broader than a classical single-gene pharmacogenetic test.

rational_drug_design_medi2004_wk7.html.title: MEDI2004 W7 · Rational Drug Design
rational_drug_design_medi2004_wk7.html.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
rational_drug_design_medi2004_wk7.html.content: How medicines are found — the shift from stumbling onto them to engineering them against a known target. Why it matters: single well-aimed molecules rewrote whole diseases. Penicillin's β-lactam ring is a reactive 'warhead' that irreversibly acylates the bacterial transpeptidase (penicillin-binding protein); because it mimics the D-Ala–D-Ala end of the cell-wall peptide the enzyme grabs it, then the strained ring jams the enzyme shut. Penicillin is selectively toxic because humans have no cell wall and no transpeptidase. In HIV, tipranavir is a protease inhibitor (blocks viral polyprotein cleavage so virions cannot mature) and maraviroc is an entry inhibitor (a CCR5 co-receptor antagonist) — hitting different points of the life-cycle. Discovery types: empirical/phenotypic (screen for an effect without knowing the target), rational/target-based (design against a defined target), and hybrid. The rational pipeline runs target hypothesis → hit → lead → lead optimisation → candidate → IND → clinical trials. Economics: each approved drug costs billions and ~10–15 years, with heavy attrition — only about 1 in 100 discovery projects reaches the market.

questions.question: Rational (target-based) drug design begins with knowledge of the drug's:
questions.explanation: Rational design starts from a defined molecular target and engineers a molecule to fit it, rather than screening blindly.

questions.question: Penicillin kills bacteria by attacking a structure that human cells do not have, the:
questions.explanation: Penicillin blocks bacterial cell-wall synthesis; humans lack a cell wall, which is why the drug is selectively toxic.

questions.question: Bringing a single new drug to market typically costs on the order of:
questions.explanation: Developing one approved drug costs billions of dollars, largely because so many candidates fail along the way.

questions.question: A protease inhibitor such as tipranavir treats HIV by blocking the virus from:
questions.explanation: HIV protease cleaves viral polyproteins into working parts; inhibiting it stops new virions from maturing.

questions.question: Empirical (phenotypic) drug discovery screens compounds for a useful effect without first knowing the:
questions.explanation: Empirical screening looks for a desired biological effect and identifies the target later, if at all.

questions.question: The reactive 'warhead' of penicillin that jams the bacterial enzyme is its:
questions.explanation: The strained four-membered β-lactam ring is highly reactive and covalently acylates the target enzyme, switching it off.

questions.question: Penicillin works because it structurally mimics the cell-wall building block:
questions.explanation: Penicillin mimics the terminal D-Ala–D-Ala of the peptidoglycan chain, so the transpeptidase binds it as if it were substrate.

questions.question: Selective toxicity means a drug harms the pathogen far more than the host by hitting a target that the host:
questions.explanation: The ideal antimicrobial hits a target unique to the pathogen (like the bacterial cell wall), sparing the host that lacks it.

questions.question: Maraviroc blocks HIV at a different step from a protease inhibitor because it prevents the virus from:
questions.explanation: Maraviroc is an entry inhibitor that antagonises the CCR5 co-receptor, stopping the virus fusing with and entering the host cell.

questions.question: Combining a protease inhibitor with an entry inhibitor in HIV is powerful because the two drugs act on:
questions.explanation: Hitting several stages of the viral life-cycle at once makes escape by resistance far harder — the logic of combination antiretroviral therapy.

questions.question: In the rational design pipeline, the first active compound found against a target is called a:
questions.explanation: A 'hit' is an initial compound showing activity against the target; it is later refined into a lead and then a candidate.

questions.question: Turning a promising hit into a lead involves chemically improving its potency, selectivity and:
questions.explanation: Lead optimisation tunes potency, selectivity and pharmacokinetic (drug-like) properties to make a molecule suitable for development.

questions.question: A hybrid discovery approach is best described as combining empirical screening with:
questions.explanation: Hybrid discovery blends phenotypic screening with rational, target-based design to draw on the strengths of both.

questions.question: Before a candidate can be tested in humans, it must gain approval to begin clinical trials, marked by the:
questions.explanation: The Investigational New Drug (IND) step authorises first-in-human testing after preclinical work supports the candidate.

questions.question: Roughly how many of every 100 drug-discovery projects finally reach the market?
questions.explanation: Attrition is severe: only about 1 in 100 discovery projects survives the funnel all the way to an approved medicine.

questions.question: The typical time from starting discovery to an approved drug is closest to:
questions.explanation: Discovery through approval usually spans about 10–15 years, reflecting the many sequential stages and failures.

questions.question: Structure-based drug design uses the three-dimensional shape of the target to design a molecule that:
questions.explanation: Knowing the target's 3D structure lets chemists design a molecule that fits its binding site precisely — the essence of rational design.

questions.question: Penicillin's block of the bacterial transpeptidase is effectively permanent because the β-lactam ring forms a bond that is:
questions.explanation: The ring acylates the enzyme's active-site serine covalently, so the block is irreversible until new enzyme is made.

questions.question: Bacteria commonly resist penicillin by producing β-lactamase, an enzyme that:
questions.explanation: β-lactamase hydrolyses the β-lactam ring before it can act, destroying the drug — a key mechanism of resistance driving side-chain redesign.

questions.question: A major advantage of rational over purely empirical discovery is that, from the start, it offers a clear:
questions.explanation: Knowing the target gives a defined mechanism that chemists can rationally optimise, unlike blind screening — though success is still not guaranteed.

questions.question: Because roughly 99 of 100 projects fail, the price of each marketed drug must effectively cover the cost of:
questions.explanation: The revenue from the one success has to pay for the 99 that failed, a central reason new medicines are so expensive.

questions.question: Targeting the CCR5 co-receptor rather than a viral enzyme means maraviroc acts on a molecule belonging to the:
questions.explanation: CCR5 is a human co-receptor the virus exploits; blocking this host protein prevents entry, a strategy distinct from hitting viral enzymes.

questions.question: Placing the stages in order, a molecule proceeds from hit to lead to:
questions.explanation: After a hit is optimised into a lead, the best lead becomes the development candidate that moves toward the IND and clinical trials.

questions.question: Designing an antiviral is often harder than an antibacterial because viruses replicate using the host's own:
questions.explanation: Viruses hijack host machinery, so there are fewer uniquely viral targets, making selective toxicity harder to achieve than with bacteria.

questions.question: Knowing a target enzyme's active-site shape most directly helps a chemist design a molecule with high:
questions.explanation: A 3D structure lets designers craft a molecule complementary to the binding site, maximising affinity and selectivity.

questions.question: The plague and HIV examples are used to show that a single new drug can change a disease's:
questions.explanation: Each case shows a drug turning a lethal disease into a treatable one — shifting the whole treatment paradigm, the payoff that justifies the cost.

questions.question: Re-engineering the penicillin side chain to defeat resistant bacteria is an early real example of:
questions.explanation: Changing one substituent to resist β-lactamase or broaden spectrum is deliberate structural modification — rational design applied to an existing scaffold.

small_molecules_vs_biologics_medi2004_wk.title: MEDI2004 W7 · Small Molecules vs Biological Drugs
small_molecules_vs_biologics_medi2004_wk.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
small_molecules_vs_biologics_medi2004_wk.content: Two drug worlds. A small-molecule drug is chemically synthesised and low in molecular weight (aspirin ≈180 Da), usually taken orally. A biological drug (biopharmaceutical/biologic) is a large active substance made by or extracted from a living organism, usually injected or infused. By prescription count the top drugs are almost all small molecules (statins, proton-pump inhibitors, metformin, antibiotics); by cost the leaders are biologics (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, dupilumab, denosumab) — few patients but very high unit price. Biologics are proteins made by recombinant DNA in expression systems such as E. coli, yeast or mammalian (CHO) cells, then purified and cold-chained. Engineering tricks include PEGylation — attaching polyethylene glycol chains to extend half-life and lower immunogenicity. Monoclonal antibodies (names ending in -mab) are made by the hybridoma method. Size dictates pharmacokinetics: a large protein cannot be swallowed (it would be digested and is too big to absorb), so it is injected; many last weeks because they clear slowly. Reproducibility differs too: a generic is an identical copy of a small molecule, whereas a biosimilar is only highly similar to its reference biologic because living systems cannot copy a large protein exactly. Newer classes include oligonucleotide and gene therapies.

questions.question: Aspirin, at roughly 180 daltons, is a typical example of a:
questions.explanation: Aspirin is a low-molecular-weight, chemically synthesised compound — the archetypal small-molecule drug.

questions.question: A biological drug is best described as a large active substance that is:
questions.explanation: Biologics are large molecules produced by or extracted from living organisms, unlike chemically synthesised small molecules.

questions.question: Most biological drugs are given by injection or infusion rather than by mouth. This route is chosen because they are:
questions.explanation: Being large proteins, biologics would be digested and cannot cross the gut wall, so they must be injected.

questions.question: A drug whose generic name ends in '-mab', such as pembrolizumab, is a:
questions.explanation: The suffix -mab marks a monoclonal antibody, a large protein biologic used widely in cancer and immune disease.

questions.question: Recombinant human insulin is produced by inserting the insulin gene into:
questions.explanation: Recombinant proteins are made by engineering living cells (such as bacteria or mammalian cells) to express the human gene.

questions.question: The single biggest physical difference between a biologic and a small molecule is its:
questions.explanation: Biologics are orders of magnitude larger than small molecules, and that size gulf drives nearly all their other differences.

questions.question: Australia's most-prescribed drugs by count are dominated by small molecules, whereas the highest-cost drugs are dominated by:
questions.explanation: Cheap oral small molecules top the prescription counts, while expensive biologics like pembrolizumab dominate the spending list.

questions.question: Complex human proteins needing sugar decoration are often made in mammalian cells such as:
questions.explanation: Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells add human-like glycosylation, so they are favoured for complex therapeutic proteins.

questions.question: Attaching polyethylene glycol chains to a protein drug (PEGylation) is done mainly to:
questions.explanation: PEGylation increases the protein's effective size and shields it, slowing clearance so the drug lasts longer and is less immunogenic.

questions.question: The classic way to produce a monoclonal antibody fuses an antibody-making B cell with a:
questions.explanation: The hybridoma fuses a B cell with an immortal myeloma cell, giving a line that both makes one antibody and divides indefinitely.

questions.question: Compared with a typical oral small molecule dosed daily, many antibody biologics are dosed only every few weeks because they:
questions.explanation: Large antibodies are eliminated slowly and have long half-lives, so effective levels persist for weeks between doses.

questions.question: A biosimilar is described as 'highly similar' rather than identical to its reference biologic because:
questions.explanation: Because a large protein is grown in living cells, it cannot be reproduced exactly, so a follow-on product is only highly similar.

questions.question: A generic of a small-molecule drug can be an exact copy of the original because the molecule is:
questions.explanation: Small molecules are made by defined chemistry, so a generic can be structurally identical — unlike a cell-grown biologic.

questions.question: Insulin must be injected rather than swallowed chiefly because in the gut it would be:
questions.explanation: As a protein, oral insulin would be broken down by digestive enzymes and is too large to absorb intact, so it is given by injection.

questions.question: Many monoclonal antibody drugs treat cancer or immune disease by binding with high specificity to a single:
questions.explanation: Monoclonal antibodies are highly selective, binding one target antigen, which underlies their precise action and clean off-target profile.

questions.question: Oligonucleotide drugs represent a newer biological class that works at the level of:
questions.explanation: Oligonucleotide therapies act on nucleic acids (such as messenger RNA), a distinct mechanism from small molecules or antibodies.

questions.question: A key reason biologics cost far more than small molecules is that they must be:
questions.explanation: Growing proteins in living cells, purifying them and keeping them refrigerated is far costlier than synthesising a small molecule.

questions.question: Why does molecular size largely dictate that biologics are injected and dosed infrequently? Because size governs their:
questions.explanation: Large size blocks gut absorption (forcing injection) and slows elimination (allowing infrequent dosing) — size drives the pharmacokinetics.

questions.question: Before approval, a biosimilar must show no clinically meaningful difference from its reference product in efficacy and:
questions.explanation: Regulators require evidence that the biosimilar matches the reference in both efficacy and safety despite minor structural variation.

questions.question: A simple non-glycosylated protein like human insulin can be made cheaply in bacteria, whereas a glycosylated antibody usually needs:
questions.explanation: Bacteria cannot add human glycosylation, so antibodies requiring it are produced in mammalian cells such as CHO lines.

questions.question: PEGylating interferon lets it be dosed weekly instead of several times a week. The best explanation is that PEG:
questions.explanation: PEG increases hydrodynamic size and shields the protein, reducing kidney clearance so the drug persists and can be given less often.

questions.question: Unlike most small molecules, protein biologics can provoke the patient to form:
questions.explanation: Being foreign proteins, biologics can trigger anti-drug antibodies that may reduce efficacy or cause reactions — a concern rare with small molecules.

questions.question: The core reason a biosimilar cannot be called a 'generic' is that its active substance is:
questions.explanation: A biologic's large, cell-made structure cannot be reproduced identically, so follow-ons are 'biosimilar', not identical generics.

questions.question: Why do the 'most prescribed' and 'most expensive' Australian drug lists barely overlap? Because common chronic conditions are treated with:
questions.explanation: High-volume chronic diseases are managed with inexpensive small molecules, while the spending list is driven by low-volume, high-price biologics.

questions.question: Gene therapies differ fundamentally from both small molecules and antibodies because they aim to:
questions.explanation: Gene therapy delivers genetic material to correct or replace a faulty gene, a mechanism distinct from blocking or binding a protein target.

questions.question: Efforts to make an oral protein drug are difficult mainly because the gut both digests protein and presents a barrier that blocks:
questions.explanation: Even if protected from digestion, a large protein cannot readily cross the intestinal epithelium, so oral biologics remain a major challenge.

questions.question: Why is batch-to-batch consistency harder for a biologic than for a small molecule? Because its production depends on:
questions.explanation: Living cell cultures introduce natural variability, so biologics need tight process control to keep batches consistent, unlike defined chemical synthesis.

drug_regulation_tga_medi2004_wk8.html.title: MEDI2004 W8 · Drug Regulation in Australia — the TGA
drug_regulation_tga_medi2004_wk8.html.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
drug_regulation_tga_medi2004_wk8.html.content: How medicines are regulated in Australia. The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) regulates therapeutic goods under the Therapeutic Goods Act; a product must be entered on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) before it can be supplied. Regulation sits at the end of the development funnel — after Phase III, before and during Phase IV. Two risk tiers: Registered medicines (AUST R) are higher-risk and evaluated for quality, safety AND efficacy (prescription drugs and many over-the-counter medicines); Listed medicines (AUST L) are lower-risk, built only from pre-approved low-risk ingredients and assessed for quality and safety but NOT efficacy (e.g. vitamins, sunscreens, many complementary medicines). New-medicine approval is evidence-based, with ongoing risk management and an approved Product Information (PI) document. Scheduling under the Poisons Standard sets how a substance is supplied: S2 Pharmacy Medicine, S3 Pharmacist Only Medicine, S4 Prescription Only Medicine, S8 Controlled Drug. The Special Access Scheme allows use of unapproved goods in defined cases; prescription medicines cannot be advertised to the public. Generics and biosimilars follow their own pathways. Importantly, TGA approval (allowed on the market) is separate from PBS listing (government subsidy of cost). Phase IV exists because rare harms (thalidomide, rofecoxib) surface only after wide use.

questions.question: In Australia, the body that regulates medicines and other therapeutic goods is the:
questions.explanation: The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) is the national regulator of medicines and therapeutic goods in Australia.

questions.question: Before a medicine can be legally supplied in Australia it must be entered on the:
questions.explanation: A product must be listed on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) before it can be supplied.

questions.question: A higher-risk medicine fully evaluated for quality, safety and efficacy carries which marking?
questions.explanation: Registered medicines carry an AUST R number, reflecting full evaluation of quality, safety and efficacy.

questions.question: A medicine that can only be obtained on a doctor's prescription is scheduled as:
questions.explanation: Schedule 4 (Prescription Only Medicine) can be supplied only on a valid prescription.

questions.question: TGA approval of a medicine means it is allowed on the market; the PBS instead decides whether it is:
questions.explanation: TGA approval permits marketing; PBS listing separately determines whether the government subsidises the medicine's cost.

questions.question: Listed (AUST L) medicines such as many vitamins are assessed for quality and safety but NOT for:
questions.explanation: Listed medicines use pre-approved low-risk ingredients and are not evaluated by the TGA for whether they actually work.

questions.question: The split between Registered and Listed medicines is fundamentally a classification by:
questions.explanation: The two tiers sort products by risk: higher-risk medicines are Registered and fully evaluated, lower-risk ones are Listed.

questions.question: The approved Product Information (PI) document for a prescription medicine is mainly intended for:
questions.explanation: The PI is the TGA-approved reference for prescribers and pharmacists, summarising indications, dosing, warnings and safety.

questions.question: A drug with high potential for abuse and dependence, tightly controlled, is scheduled as:
questions.explanation: Schedule 8 (Controlled Drug) covers substances like strong opioids that need strict recording and control.

questions.question: The document that assigns each substance to a schedule is the:
questions.explanation: The Poisons Standard (SUSMP) sets the schedule for each substance, determining how it may be supplied.

questions.question: A medicine that a pharmacist must personally hand over after assessing the customer is scheduled:
questions.explanation: Schedule 3 (Pharmacist Only Medicine) requires the pharmacist's involvement but not a prescription.

questions.question: Under Australian rules, prescription (S4) medicines may NOT be advertised directly to:
questions.explanation: Direct-to-consumer advertising of prescription medicines is prohibited; promotion is restricted to health professionals.

questions.question: The Special Access Scheme allows a patient to receive a medicine that is:
questions.explanation: The Special Access Scheme permits supply of unapproved therapeutic goods for individual patients in defined circumstances.

questions.question: In the drug-development funnel, the TGA's approval decision falls after Phase III and just before:
questions.explanation: Regulatory approval is the last narrow point of the funnel, after the pivotal Phase III trials and before Phase IV monitoring.

questions.question: A generic medicine entering the market must still be entered on the ARTG and shown to be:
questions.explanation: A generic must demonstrate bioequivalence to the reference product and be registered before it can be supplied.

questions.question: The TGA's decision to approve a new medicine is based primarily on:
questions.explanation: Approval rests on the evidence dossier — quality, safety and efficacy data — not on reputation or popularity.

questions.question: A sunscreen marked AUST L and an antibiotic marked AUST R differ most importantly in whether the TGA assessed their:
questions.explanation: Registered (AUST R) products are evaluated for efficacy; Listed (AUST L) products are not, being lower-risk pre-approved ingredients.

questions.question: A new cancer drug is TGA-approved but not PBS-listed. For patients this most likely means the drug is:
questions.explanation: TGA approval lets it be sold, but without PBS subsidy the patient bears the high cost until (or unless) it is listed.

questions.question: A separate regulatory-approval step exists mainly because the company that developed the drug is:
questions.explanation: After years and a fortune invested, the developer cannot rule impartially on its own product, so an independent TGA gate is required.

questions.question: Drugs like thalidomide and rofecoxib show why post-marketing surveillance matters: some harms appear only once the drug reaches:
questions.explanation: Rare or delayed harms surface only when millions are exposed after approval, which is exactly what Phase IV surveillance is designed to catch.

questions.question: Moving a substance from S4 to S3 would generally make it:
questions.explanation: S3 (Pharmacist Only) needs no prescription, so down-scheduling from S4 to S3 increases access under pharmacist supervision.

questions.question: For a prescriber, 'TGA-approved' should be read as meaning the benefit–risk balance looked acceptable, not that the drug is:
questions.explanation: Approval reflects an acceptable benefit–risk judgement on current evidence; it never guarantees zero risk, hence continued vigilance.

questions.question: A biosimilar is regulated differently from a small-molecule generic because its active substance:
questions.explanation: A biologic cannot be reproduced identically, so a biosimilar follows a distinct pathway proving high similarity rather than identity.

questions.question: The legal authority making ARTG entry and TGA oversight compulsory comes from the:
questions.explanation: The Therapeutic Goods Act is the legislation underpinning the TGA, the ARTG and the compulsory regulation of therapeutic goods.

questions.question: Ongoing risk-management requirements after approval reflect that regulation does not stop at the:
questions.explanation: Risk-management plans and Phase IV monitoring continue after approval, showing that oversight extends well beyond the approval decision.

questions.question: A company wanting to make a strong efficacy claim for a herbal product could not simply List it, because Listed medicines may only use:
questions.explanation: Listing is confined to pre-approved low-risk ingredients and permits only limited claims; a strong efficacy claim would require Registration.

mutations_repair_medi2200_wk8.html.title: Mutations & DNA Repair
mutations_repair_medi2200_wk8.html.subject: Human Cell & Molecular Biology
mutations_repair_medi2200_wk8.html.content: MEDI2200 Week 8 covers how DNA changes (mutation) and how it is mended (repair): the germline/somatic distinction, single-gene mutations and their protein effects, chromosome-number and structural mutations, the types of DNA damage, and the four repair pathways (mismatch, base-excision, nucleotide-excision, and double-strand-break repair).

questions.question: Which statement best defines a mutation as used in this module?
options: A. A temporary chemical modification of a DNA base that is always reversed
B. A change confined to RNA that never affects the DNA sequence
C. A permanent change in the amount or structure of genetic material
D. Any variation in protein folding after translation
questions.explanation: A mutation is a permanent change in the amount or structure of DNA. Reversible chemical modifications are 'damage', not yet a mutation, and mutations are DNA-level, not purely post-translational.

questions.question: A mutation arises in a skin cell of an adult. What is the most accurate consequence?
options: A. It is germline and will be inherited by all offspring
B. It is somatic and will not be passed to that person's children
C. It will be corrected because somatic cells cannot tolerate mutations
D. It converts the cell's germline into somatic tissue
questions.explanation: A skin cell is somatic, so the change cannot enter the gametes and is not heritable — though it can still affect that individual (e.g. cancer).

questions.question: Regarding genetic variation between and within individuals, which is correct?
options: A. It is rare, and nearly all mutations cause disease
B. It occurs only in germline cells
C. It is very common, and most mutations are harmless
D. It is limited to people with an inherited disorder
questions.explanation: Variation between people and even between cells of one person is very common; the vast majority of mutations have no effect on gene function or phenotype.

questions.question: A single nucleotide is replaced by another with no net gain or loss of DNA. What is this?
questions.explanation: A substitution swaps one base for another without changing the length; insertions and deletions change the amount of DNA.

questions.question: A point mutation that leaves the amino-acid sequence of the protein unchanged is described as:
questions.explanation: A silent mutation changes a base but the codon still specifies the same amino acid, so the protein is unchanged.

questions.question: A complete normal human karyotype consists of:
options: A. 46 chromosomes — 23 pairs of autosomes and no sex chromosomes
B. 23 chromosomes — one of each type
C. 44 chromosomes — 22 pairs of autosomes only
D. 46 chromosomes — 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes
questions.explanation: Humans have 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of sex chromosomes.

questions.question: The most common cause of aneuploidy is:
options: B. Replication slippage at a triplet repeat
questions.explanation: Aneuploidy (abnormal chromosome number) most commonly results from nondisjunction — failure of chromosomes to segregate in meiosis.

questions.question: Which enzyme performs the final step shared by the excision repair pathways?
options: A. DNA glycosylase, which removes the base
B. An excision nuclease, which cuts the strand
C. DNA ligase, which seals the remaining nick
D. A helicase, which unwinds the duplex
questions.explanation: After excision and polymerase fill-in, DNA ligase seals the nick to restore the backbone. The other enzymes act earlier in the pathway.

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a common type of DNA damage?
questions.explanation: Depurination, deamination, thymine dimers, alkylation and adducts are the damage types given. The others are normal cellular events, not DNA damage.

questions.question: An insertion of nucleotides alters the downstream amino-acid sequence only when the number of bases inserted is:
options: A. Not a multiple of three
questions.explanation: Codons are read in triplets; only indels that are not a multiple of three shift the reading frame. A three-base insertion adds a whole codon without shifting the frame.

questions.question: A nonsense mutation is most likely to have which effect on the gene's product?
options: A. A truncated transcript that is usually degraded, yielding no protein
B. A full-length protein with one substituted amino acid
C. A protein identical to normal because the code is redundant
D. A longer-than-normal protein that reads through the stop codon
questions.explanation: A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon; the truncated mRNA is typically degraded and no protein is made. One substituted residue describes missense; an unchanged protein describes silent.

questions.question: Single-nucleotide substitutions arise most commonly from which spontaneous event?
options: A. Replication slippage over a trinucleotide repeat
B. Deamination of methylated cytosine to thymine
C. Formation of a bulky adduct on guanine
questions.explanation: Although substitutions can come from replication or repair errors, they most commonly arise from spontaneous deamination of methylated cytosine to thymine. The other options describe indels, adduct damage, and a chromosome-number error.

questions.question: In Huntington's disease, why do symptoms tend to appear earlier in successive generations?
options: A. Triplet repeats expand across generations; longer runs, earlier onset
B. The missense substitution becomes more severe as the protein ages
C. Somatic mutations accumulate equally in every family member
D. Each generation gains an extra whole chromosome
questions.explanation: CAG repeats over ~28 are unstable and expand across generations; because more repeats correlate with earlier onset, the disease shows anticipation. Huntington's is a repeat-expansion disorder, not a simple missense or aneuploidy.

questions.question: A mutation in the sequence at an intron-exon boundary would most directly cause:
options: A. A premature stop codon in the middle of an exon
B. An extra chromosome in the gamete
C. Mature mRNA that retains an intron or is missing an exon
D. Loss of the gene's promoter and no transcription
questions.explanation: Splice-site sequences guide the spliceosome; mutating them causes intron retention or exon skipping in the mature transcript. A premature stop is nonsense, and the other options are unrelated to splicing.

questions.question: A mutant allele produces an abnormal protein that binds and inactivates the normal protein from the other allele. This is best classified as:
questions.explanation: A dominant-negative product interferes with the normal protein. Loss-of-function simply reduces or eliminates product; gain-of-function adds novel or excess product.

questions.question: A gamete that received both copies of a chromosome after nondisjunction is fertilised by a normal gamete. The offspring will be:
options: C. Balanced with a normal karyotype
D. Haploid for the whole genome
questions.explanation: A gamete carrying two copies plus one normal copy gives three copies — trisomy. The partner gamete that received none would give monosomy.

questions.question: Which best distinguishes a balanced from an unbalanced structural rearrangement?
options: A. A balanced rearrangement always changes the total chromosome number
B. An unbalanced rearrangement never affects the phenotype
C. A balanced rearrangement has no net gain or loss of chromosomal material
D. An unbalanced rearrangement occurs only in somatic cells
questions.explanation: Balanced means the material is rearranged with no net gain or loss; unbalanced means a gain or loss of material, which is more likely to affect phenotype.

questions.question: Mismatch repair must decide which strand to correct. In eukaryotes, the strand to be repaired is identified because it:
options: A. Is the more heavily methylated of the two strands
B. Carries transient nicks that mark it as the new strand
C. Contains uracil instead of thymine
D. Is always the strand running 5' to 3' left to right
questions.explanation: Nicks in the new strand (from Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand, and leading-strand joins) flag it as the error-containing daughter strand to repair.

questions.question: Which enzyme initiates base excision repair by recognising and removing a specific damaged base?
questions.explanation: A DNA glycosylase recognises a particular damaged base and cleaves it from the sugar, leaving an abasic site. Excision nuclease acts in NER, Ku in NHEJ, and ligase seals at the end.

questions.question: Which lesion would be handled by nucleotide excision repair rather than base excision repair?
options: A. A single deaminated cytosine base (uracil)
B. A single oxidised guanine (8-oxoG) base
C. A UV-induced pyrimidine dimer that distorts the helix
D. A single alkylated base such as 3-methyladenine
questions.explanation: NER handles bulky, helix-distorting damage such as UV dimers and large adducts. Single-base chemical lesions (deamination, oxidation, alkylation) are BER substrates.

questions.question: Non-homologous end joining, rather than homologous recombination, predominates in which situation?
options: A. In late S and G2, when sister chromatids are close together
B. Whenever the break is in a gene-coding region
C. In G1 and early S phase, before a sister chromatid is available
D. Only in germline cells during meiosis
questions.explanation: NHEJ predominates in G1/early S because there is no identical sister chromatid to template from; HR becomes important in late S/G2 when sisters are present.

questions.question: Why is non-homologous end joining considered error-prone?
options: A. It copies the wrong sister chromatid as a template
B. Trimming the broken ends before ligation loses nucleotides
C. It leaves the break unsealed until the next cell cycle
D. It inserts uracil in place of thymine at the junction
questions.explanation: NHEJ rejoins ends without a template, and the nuclease clean-up always loses nucleotides — harmless unless the loss falls in a coding or regulatory region, and unrelated ends can be joined to make translocations.

questions.question: Sickle-cell disease results from a single A-to-T substitution that replaces glutamate with valine in β-globin. Which class of mutation, and via which immediate mechanism, does this represent?
options: A. Nonsense — the altered codon becomes a premature stop
B. Missense — the codon now specifies a different amino acid
C. Frameshift — the reading frame shifts from the substituted base onward
D. Silent — the substitution leaves the amino-acid sequence unchanged
questions.explanation: A base swap that changes one amino acid (Glu→Val) is a missense mutation. It does not create a stop codon (nonsense), shift the frame (a substitution keeps length constant), or leave the sequence unchanged (silent).

questions.question: Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome) is driven by loss of which repair function, and through which proteins?
options: A. Nucleotide excision repair, via helix-distortion sensors
B. Homologous recombination, via BRCA1 and BRCA2
C. Base excision repair, via a uracil DNA glycosylase
D. Mismatch repair, via the human MutS and MutL homologues
questions.explanation: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) arises from mutations in the human versions of MutS and MutL, crippling mismatch repair and raising mutation rates over 100-fold. NER loss gives xeroderma pigmentosum; HR loss underlies BRCA cancers.

questions.question: A child is extremely sensitive to sunlight and develops multiple early skin cancers; several NER genes are mutated. The most direct reason UV exposure is so mutagenic in this patient is that:
options: A. Ionising radiation directly breaks both DNA strands that cannot be rejoined
B. Pyrimidine dimers cannot be excised, so they persist and are copied into mutations
C. Cytosine deamination is no longer reversed by glycosylases
D. Mismatches escape proofreading because the new strand lacks nicks
questions.explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum is an NER defect; UV pyrimidine dimers can't be removed, so they distort the helix and are converted to mutations on replication. The other options describe DSB repair, BER, and MMR — different pathways.

questions.question: If deamination of a cytosine is not repaired before the strand is replicated, what is the resulting change in the daughter DNA?
options: A. A former G–C pair becomes an A–T pair (a substitution)
B. A base pair is deleted, shortening the strand
C. An extra base pair is inserted at the site
D. Both strands are broken at the lesion
questions.explanation: Deaminated cytosine reads as uracil/thymine-like, so replication places an adenine opposite it, converting the original G–C to A–T — a substitution. Depurination, not deamination, tends to cause deletions.

questions.question: In a balanced-translocation carrier, which segregation pattern of the meiotic quadrivalent can yield balanced (normal-phenotype) gametes?
options: C. Any of the three patterns equally
questions.explanation: Only alternate segregation produces balanced gametes; adjacent-1 and adjacent-2 both yield only unbalanced gametes, which is why carriers have reduced fertility.

questions.question: Homologous recombination repairs a double-strand break accurately because it:
options: A. Directly religates the two broken ends without processing them
B. Removes a 12-nucleotide stretch and resynthesises from the same strand
C. Excises a single damaged base and fills the one-nucleotide gap
D. Copies the undamaged sister chromatid as a template
questions.explanation: HR resects the 5' ends, the 3' end invades the intact sister chromatid, and the lost sequence is copied back accurately. Direct religation is NHEJ; the 12-nt patch is NER; the single-base fill is BER.

questions.question: Double-strand breaks are considered especially hazardous compared with single-base damage mainly because:
options: A. Both strands are cut at once, risking loss or translocations
B. They can only ever be repaired during G1 phase
C. They convert every downstream codon into a stop codon
D. They are undetectable by any cellular sensor
questions.explanation: With both strands cut there is no intact template at the break, so material can be lost and unrelated ends can be joined into translocations. They are detected and repaired by NHEJ or HR depending on cell-cycle phase.

questions.question: Cells carrying an inherited BRCA1 or BRCA2 loss-of-function mutation are prone to genomic instability primarily because they:
options: A. Cannot excise UV pyrimidine dimers
B. Cannot remove mismatched bases from the new strand
C. Cannot deaminate cytosine during normal metabolism
D. Cannot perform accurate homologous recombination of breaks
questions.explanation: BRCA1/2 are required for homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks; without them cells rely on error-prone NHEJ, accumulating deletions and translocations that drive breast/ovarian cancer. The other options describe NER and MMR defects.

questions.question: Which statement best captures why a repaired chemical lesion does not become a mutation, whereas an unrepaired one may?
options: A. A lesion becomes a mutation only when replication copies it
B. A lesion is a mutation the instant it forms, regardless of replication
C. Repair enzymes convert lesions into mutations to preserve information
D. Only lesions in germline cells can ever become mutations
questions.explanation: Damage is a reversible chemical change; it becomes a permanent, base-paired mutation only if replication reads the damaged template before repair. That deadline is why repair races replication.
